    3 - 23 · FUEL SYSTEMSR

    FUEL FEEDBACK

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    CLOSED LOOP FUEL CONTROL

    In CLOSED LOOP modes the PCM fine-tunes injector pulse width from the upstream heated oxygen sensor inputs (Fig. 1). The software performs this work in two bank trim routines, one for each cylinder bank: 011DF0 for bank 1 and 0128CA for bank 2. Bank 1 reads its upstream oxygen value from F8038; bank 2 reads F803A.

    The fuel pulse width routine (0109DC) calls both trim routines after it has selected the base fuel value (3-1 Fuel Amount). Each call is enabled by a configuration bit in ROM 270A: bit 80 enables the bank 1 routine and bit 20 enables the bank 2 routine (Fig. 2). This calibration stores A1, so both banks run. When RAM flag F8558 bit 10 is set, the bank 2 call also requires ROM 270D bit 40 to be clear; this calibration stores 00 at that address, so the call is always made.

    The short-term correction for each bank is held in F828C (bank 1) and F828D (bank 2), and the long-term correction in F827E (bank 1) and F8280 (bank 2). The diagnostic data services report these four values as standard parameters 06 to 09, and report the two upstream oxygen values with their short-term corrections as parameters 14 and 18.

    LEARNING GATE AND FEEDBACK CONDITIONS

    Each bank trim routine opens with a learning gate (Fig. 4). The gate tests the shared upstream inhibit flag F8880 bit 02 together with stored fault-state fields at F880C, F880D and F880E. When the inhibit flag or a selected F880D bit is set, the routine sets its inhibit marker (F8175 bit 08 for bank 1, F8176 bit 08 for bank 2). On any gate condition, the routine clears the bank's 27 learned entries (F889A for bank 1, F88B5 for bank 2) and branches to its fallback path. The fallback path clears the short-term correction and resets the working terms of the bank.

    With the gate passed, the routine qualifies the upstream oxygen value. A value below 3E (ROM 3348) reloads a holdoff count from ROM 334E (bank 2: ROM 334F). A value at or above the limit sends the routine to the fallback path once the holdoff count is zero.

    Engine speed is tested next, with hysteresis. Above 3808 rpm the routine sets its speed flag (F82D4 bit 01 for bank 1, F82D5 bit 01 for bank 2) and takes the fallback path. The flag clears only after engine speed falls to 96 rpm below the limit. Further state tests follow. Most divert the routine to the fallback path; two of them instead load a fixed short-term correction from ROM 338D or ROM 3352 and reset the working terms.

    SHORT-TERM CORRECTION

    The qualified oxygen value is converted through the curve at ROM 3704, shared by both banks, and the result (F8292 for bank 1, F8293 for bank 2) is compared with the bank's switching targets. One of those targets is the rear target value F828E (bank 2: F828F), written by the rear target routines 01D386 and 01D67E. The outcome of the comparison is held in the bank's feedback state byte, F82D4 or F82D5. Bit 02 of F82D4 is the bank 1 feedback state that the purge oxygen sequence also reads (5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs).

    Normal rear feedback is enabled by ROM 270A bit 40 for bank 1 and bit 10 for bank 2. Both bits are clear in this calibration, so the rear target routines run their fallback target handling.

    The short-term correction is the signed sum of three working terms, F82A2, F8290 and F8286. The third term is the difference of two working values multiplied by the gain in ROM 35A3. The sum is limited to the range set by ROM 35AC and ROM 35AE for bank 1, and ROM 35AD and ROM 35AF for bank 2, before it is stored (Fig. 5).

    OXYGEN SENSOR STATE AND HEATER HISTORY

    Two jobs in the fast supporting group (01FCF6) maintain the oxygen sensor state that the trim routines and monitors consume (1-6 Supporting Jobs).

    The threshold tracking routine (0163C6) watches the rear bank 1 input F803C. A reading below 3D sets low flag F8568 bit 40 once its holdoff count, reloaded from ROM 7B82 (2), has expired; a reading at or above the threshold clears the flag and reloads the count. While the engine is running, the routine latches a low-to-high crossing of each enabled input: a reading below 0F arms the crossing, and a later reading at or above 28 completes it (Fig. 6). The bank 1 upstream crossing is always tracked; the rear bank 1 crossing is enabled by ROM 270A bit 20, which is set in this calibration.

    The heater history routine (019B54) reads the stored history of the four oxygen sensor heater codes and sets two shared inhibit flags. The upstream heater codes, P0135 and P0155, set F8880 bit 02, which the learning gate of both bank trim routines tests. The downstream heater codes, P0141 and P0161, set F8880 bit 01, which the rear target routines test. The routine recognizes exact combined history patterns: on every pass it sets each flag when its pattern is recognized and clears it otherwise.

    The ASD relay supplies battery voltage to the upstream and downstream heated oxygen sensor heaters. The upstream sensor signals reach the PCM on circuits K241 and K41 (Fig. 7).

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    FUEL SYSTEM MONITOR

    The fuel system monitor compares the short-term correction, combined with the long-term (adaptive) memory, against a limit (Fig. 8). In the software this is the rich/lean trim monitor 01C512, attached to descriptor C02E. It tests pressure, running and feedback state, then compares the signed long-term and short-term corrections of each bank (F827E with F828C, and F8280 with F828D) through staged countdowns. Its result bits 01, 02, 04 and 08 at F8157 select fault codes P0172, P0171, P0175 and P0174 through the code list at ROM 6DDE. The selector 0151D2 takes the lowest remaining result bit and returns its fault id for recording (8-2 Fault Reporting).

    MONITOR DESCRIPTORS

    The detailed fault-monitor descriptors (Fig. 10) decide which monitor families the PCM schedules (8-1 Diagnostic Overview). In this calibration the enable mask allows the fuel system monitor (C02E). The oxygen-response descriptors C066 (018078, codes P0133, P0153, P0139) and C082 (0183EE, codes P0139, P0159) are not allowed, so their routines are not scheduled.

    SR4 · IGNITION SYSTEM4 - 1

    SPARK TIMING

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    IGNITION SYSTEM

    The Viper uses a distributorless ignition system with two coil packs at the rear of the engine. The left pack holds three coils and the right pack holds two; each coil fires two cylinders at once, one on its compression stroke and one on its exhaust stroke (Fig. 9). The PCM grounds each coil through its own driver circuit on connector C3. Basic ignition timing is not adjustable: the PCM sets spark advance from intake air temperature, coolant temperature, engine speed, manifold vacuum and throttle position (Fig. 1).

    The PCM software calculates a single spark advance value and hands it to the output system as command 24. The value is kept in half-degree counts before top dead center. The calculation runs as an engine-event task: each event whose profile entry carries bit 01 dispatches spark initialization (0100E8) while the spark-initialization phase flag F80D1 bit 20 is set, and the spark advance calculation (01015A) at all other times. Refer to 1-3 Job Scheduling and 2-1 Engine Position and Timing.

    SPARK MODES

    Two mode flags in F80D4 choose the primary spark source before any correction is applied (Fig. 3).

    Closed-throttle low-speed mode (bit 10). With the throttle at its closed reference, the mode sets when the engine speed byte (32 rpm per count) is at or below 46, and holds until the byte exceeds that value plus 3. Opening the throttle clears the mode. Entering the mode, or leaving it through the throttle, sets the transition request F80D5 bit 20. In this mode the primary source is the coolant curve at 2778 or 278B (Fig. 11).

    Timed post-start mode (bit 40). Spark initialization clears the ramp value F83D3 and sends command 24 with a zero payload, or FF when F80D5 bit 80 is pending. It then arms the post-start mode when coolant temperature is from 10 °C up to 30 °C, loading the post-start timer F83E0 with 64 counts. The timer counts down only after the post-crank qualification flag F80D1 bit 10 is set. When it reaches zero the mode clears and the end-of-mode request F80D5 bit 40 is set. In this mode the primary source is the speed and pressure grid at 2995 (Fig. 10).

    BIT 10BIT 40PRIMARY SPARK SOURCE

    SetClearCoolant curve 2778 or 278B

    BASE SPARK AND CORRECTIONS

    Engine speed and filtered manifold pressure enter the spark grids as coordinates F8170 and F816F, on a 17-point speed axis and a 9-point pressure axis. With neither mode flag set, the routine reads one of two base maps, 285D and 28F9 (Fig. 5), and stores the result in F83DB. Map 285D is used whenever F880B bit 01 or bit 04 is set; otherwise the choice follows the countdown F80AB and the state bit F80CB bit 10 (Fig. 4). In this calibration the two maps hold identical values. When the throttle-duration flag F80D4 bit 04 is set, the grid at 2A31 is added to the base value; the flag sets after the larger-opening throttle qualifier has persisted for more than 8 passes. Every cell of 2A31 is zero in this calibration.

    When F80D4 bit 20 is set, two temperature corrections follow. Coolant temperature selects a row of grid 2ACD and intake air temperature a row of grid 2B21 (Fig. 12, Fig. 13); both use the pressure coordinate for the column. Their signed sum, saturated at 80 and 7E, is stored in F83DE. The fixed combined-mode value skips both corrections.

    SPARK TARGET AND LIMITS

    The routine adds the primary source, the base value, the post-start value, the temperature correction and the signed term F83E1. The running sum is set to 7E when the primary source and base value together reach 7F or when the last addition overflows, and to zero whenever an addition turns it negative. It then subtracts two retard terms, each with a floor of zero: a calibrated retard F83E5, and the shift-torque retard F8457 produced by 024AF4. The shift-torque path is enabled by ROM A009 bit 40, which is clear in this calibration (6-2 Transmission Controls). The result is the spark target F83D5 (Fig. 6).

    A transition stage then carries the delivered value F83D6 toward the target. The low-speed mode request (F80D5 bit 20) and the end-of-post-start request (F80D5 bit 40) both route through this stage, which moves the value in calibrated steps rather than in one jump.

    When its enable flag F80D4 bit 08 is set, the routine also computes an idle speed term. It takes the difference between engine speed F805A and the idle speed target F811C, in 2 rpm counts limited to FF, and reads curve 27C8 at or above the target or 27A2 below it (Fig. 14); ROM 270B bit 80 is set in this calibration and selects these two curves. The signed result F83DC is added to the delivered value, again held between 0 and 7E.

    OVERRIDES, RUNUP AND COMMAND

    Three override flags replace the calculated value outright: F8109 bit 02 substitutes F834A, F8109 bit 80 substitutes 28 half-degree counts, and F8128 bit 80 substitutes the value at ROM 403A. Without an override, while the runup flag F80D1 bit 08 is set, the ramp value F83D3 rises by 22 counts on each pass and is delivered in place of the target until it comes within two counts of it; the flag then clears and the target is delivered.

    The final value is stored in F83D9, which the diagnostic timing-advance report (Mode 01 PID 0E) reads. The routine shifts it right one bit, so the command carries whole degrees, and queues it as command 24 with select 1E (Fig. 7). The coprocessor command service (029270) writes command 24 directly to transmit word FFD22 and sets pending bit 80, bypassing the general queue. Refer to 5-1 Output Commands.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    IGNITION TIMING

    Basic ignition timing is not adjustable. To check the commanded value, read the timing-advance parameter with a scan tool; it reports F83D9 in half-degree resolution. Engine speed, coolant temperature, intake air temperature, manifold pressure and throttle position all change the commanded value. Check those inputs first when timing is out of range. Refer to 7-1 Substitute Values.

    DIAGNOSTIC TROUBLE CODES

    The PCM monitors the primary circuit of each coil. A code sets when peak primary current is not reached within maximum dwell time (Fig. 15, Fig. 16). The PCM cannot detect an inoperative coil, fouled or worn spark plugs, cross firing, or open spark plug cables.

    SR5 · PCM OUTPUTS5 - 1

    OUTPUT COMMANDS

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    OUTPUT REQUESTS

    The PCM software separates the decision to operate an output from the command that operates it. Each control routine records its decision as a request bit in RAM. A separate output stage converts the requests into commands and passes the commands to the PCM output hardware. The service manual lists the outputs the PCM operates (Fig. 1).

    Three request bytes, F8106, F8107 and F8108, hold the on/off requests that leave the processor through the command queue. A fourth byte, F8502, holds requests that are presented directly on a processor port (refer to Shared Port Outputs). Fuel pulse width and spark advance travel on their own command path (refer to Fuel and Spark Commands). The reset routine (020000) writes all four request bytes before the job schedule starts.

    Each request bit has a normal control routine, and all but the malfunction indicator lamp bit have DRB test routines that write it, as listed below. The engine-event loss path (013D90) sets F8106 bits 40 and 80 when engine events stop, and the first engine event clears them again (2-2 Loss of Engine Events). Because ROM 2708 bit 40 is clear (08), the same paths also set and clear F8108 bit 04.

    CHANGED-OUTPUT SERVICE

    The changed-output service (029AFC) is the last call of the fast engine-control job group (01FC8E), so it runs after every control routine in that group has updated its requests (1-3 Job Scheduling). It handles the three request bytes in order, F8106, F8107, then F8108 (Fig. 2).

    For each byte the service first checks the command queue. When the queue already holds nine commands, the service returns and the remaining bytes wait for the next pass. Otherwise it forms the payload from the request byte and compares the payload with its shadow byte. An unchanged payload sends nothing. A changed payload is copied to the shadow and queued as that byte's command (Fig. 3).

    REQUESTSHADOWCOMMANDSELECT
    F8106F8103041E
    F8107F8104261E
    F8108F8105041D

    The shadow is written only when the command is queued, so a change held back by a full queue is sent on a later pass. A request that a control routine sets and clears again between two passes produces no command. The shadow bytes record the last payload queued for each request byte.

    Until the engine has run, the service sends each byte with a startup mask applied: the payload is the request byte ANDed with the complement of ROM 270E, 270F or 2710. The service sets the pass-through latch, F811F bit 02, when the engine-running flag F80D1 bit 40 is set or the high byte of the engine-running timer F8096 is nonzero. With the latch set, the request bytes pass unmasked. The service sets this latch and never clears it.

    The F8107 mask is 90. Before the latch sets, the shift indicator lamp bit 80 and the malfunction indicator lamp bit 10 are sent clear. The skip-shift solenoid bit 08 passes in both cases (Fig. 4).

    COMMAND QUEUE AND TRANSFER

    The command queue routine (029270, entered through 010028) receives a command record: a command number, a destination select and a payload. It files the record by command number. Command 24 (spark) has a dedicated one-word slot. Commands 13 (fuel) and 19 fill a dedicated two-word slot, with the command number increased by one for the second word. Command 15 has a dedicated three-word slot and two holding records at F8120 and F8124 for use while that slot is busy.

    All other commands enter the general queue. The queue holds nine entries; the count is F80E4 and the write index is F80E2. Each entry is a transmit word, the command number and payload, in QSPI transmit RAM at FFD2E, and its destination select in QSPI command RAM at FFD47. The select byte chooses which peripheral receives the word. When the queue already holds nine entries, the record is not stored. Commands 01, 03 and 45–47 also record the RAM address that receives the returned data.

    The QSPI service (0293F6, entered through 01002C) moves commands to the hardware. Flag F80CC bit 80 prevents a second entry while the service runs. The service sends the dedicated three-word, fuel and spark slots before it takes an entry from the general queue, and loads the QSPI queue pointers for each transfer. It is called from the reset routine, the pending-task dispatcher (028992), the vehicle-speed and serial interrupt (01E14E), the level-5 interrupt (029F90) and the engine-event capture interrupt (028F24), which queues a prepared fuel word and starts the transfer itself.

    FUEL AND SPARK COMMANDS

    Fuel and spark do not pass through the changed-output service. The fuel controller (0109DC) packs the pulse width into command 13 with the high byte and command 14 with the low byte, both to select 1D. The spark controller (01015A) sends command 24 to select 1E; the payload is the advance in whole degrees, formed by halving the internal half-degree value. Refer to 3-1 Fuel Amount and 4-1 Spark Timing.

    The fuel controller indexes a table of ten one-bit output masks with its fuel cursor F811E (Fig. 5). The mask bits follow the firing order of the selected V10 profile, 1-10-9-4-3-6-5-8-7-2, rotated by one position. The service manual places all ten injector drivers on connector C2 and documents sequential injection.

    SHARED PORT OUTPUTS

    The fast vehicle-state job group (01FC58) presents F8502 bits 08, 10, 20 and 40 on the timer general-purpose port. The present routine (01A02A) copies those four request bits into the port data register at FF907 without inversion and sets the same four bits of the data-direction register at FF906, making them outputs (Fig. 6). Later in the same group, the release routine (01A04A) clears the four direction bits and returns the pins to inputs.

    The port is read back and compared with the request. The mismatch routine (01A058) compares port bits 20 and 40 with F8502 and latches each disagreement in F84FE when the bit was requested set, or in F84FF when it was requested clear. A second routine (01A138) compares bits 08 and 10 and latches F8496 bits 01 and 02. The reverse lockout request uses this path (6-3 Reverse Lockout), as do the speed control vacuum and vent requests (5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs).

    AUTOMATIC SHUTDOWN RELAY

    The service manual documents the ASD relay as a PCM ground-side output that supplies the fuel injectors, ignition coils and oxygen sensor heaters, and that the PCM de-energizes when crankshaft and camshaft signals are absent (Fig. 7). In the software, the engine-event loss path sets F8106 bits 40 and 80 and queues command 04 to select 1E with the new byte. The recovery path (013DAE) clears the same bits and queues the same command. Both paths also queue command 2D and copy F8106 to its shadow F8103 themselves, so the changed-output service does not send the byte a second time (2-2 Loss of Engine Events).

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    DRB OUTPUT TESTS

    The DRB actuator tests are dispatched through a table of 69 handler slots (Fig. 8). Each output test changes the same request bit that normal control writes (refer to Output Requests). For a bit in F8106, F8107 or F8108, the changed-output service then queues the new byte exactly as it does for a control routine, so a test exercises the complete command path. A bit in F8502 reaches the processor port through the shared port routines. The diagnostic timeout service (01F2E2) counts down F834C. When the count ends with F8128 bit 08 set, it clears that bit and calls the actuator dispatch (00CF96); with F8128 bit 04 set, it calls the output restore routine (00DCAE).

    DIAGNOSTIC TROUBLE CODES

    The PCM monitors its output circuits. An open or shorted circuit sets the codes shown in Fig. 9, Fig. 10 and Fig. 11. Codes for the A/C clutch relay and EVAP purge solenoid circuits are listed in 5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs.

    ACCESSORY AND EVAPORATIVE OUTPUTS

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    A/C CLUTCH CONTROL

    The PCM controls the A/C compressor clutch through a request that the A/C clutch control routine (018588) updates on each pass of the fast job schedule. The routine combines engine running state, the A/C switch request, throttle position, engine speed, coolant temperature and several timers before it changes the request (Fig. 1).

    Engine speed and coolant temperature are each tested against a pair of calibrated limits (Fig. 3). Each limit flag sets beyond its upper value and clears only past its lower value, so the flag does not cycle at the boundary. A low-speed flag sets below 480 rpm and is held by a calibrated timer once speed reaches 512 rpm. Refer to Specifications.

    The clutch request is stored at F8107, bit 20. The DRB A/C clutch relay test (00E4BE) operates the same bit. When the request changes, the changed-output service (029AFC) queues it (5-1 Output Commands). The PCM grounds the A/C clutch relay coil on circuit C13 at PCM cavity C1-1 (Fig. 2).

    A/C IDLE AIR CORRECTION

    The A/C clutch control routine sets and clears F810A bit 40. When bit 40 differs from bit 80 and the delay count has expired, the A/C transition service (021D28) toggles bit 80 and applies a calibrated correction (021DA8) to the requested idle air position. When the hold count that follows reaches zero, a follow-up correction (021E7C) runs once. The idle air control service (021960) runs the transition service on running passes before its speed correction (5-3 Idle Air Control).

    EVAP PURGE CONTROL

    The EVAP purge solenoid controls the vacuum source for the EVAP canister. The PCM operates the solenoid by switching its ground on circuit K52 at PCM cavity C1-20. When energized, the solenoid blocks vacuum to the canister. When de-energized, the canister purges to the throttle body (Fig. 4).

    The purge control routine (014386) runs in the fast job schedule. Before shaping a request it checks engine running state, coolant temperature, fuel-control state, timers and inhibit flags. A separate override flag transfers the request to the purge sequences described below.

    The purge target is built from a calculated load value, curve lookups and a delayed ramp. The load value (014780) is computed from engine speed and the base fuel value, and is limited to FF. The ramp (014620) moves the request gradually toward its target. A new request is sent only when it has changed and the command queue has room. At shutdown, a countdown service (0147A6) sends a zero request.

    The DRB EVAP purge solenoid test (00E522) uses the same output command and request field (Fig. 5).

    K52 CIRCUITSOLENOIDCANISTER
    Grounded by PCMEnergizedVacuum blocked
    Ground releasedDe-energizedPurges to throttle body

    PURGE SEQUENCES

    Two additional sequences can drive the purge output. The oxygen-feedback sequence (01DF10) takes over the purge request while the normal path is bypassed. It steps the request using pressure change, oxygen-feedback state and stored limits.

    The purge-response sequence (01E2FC) filters bank 1 fuel trim (01E4B8), compares it with a baseline, and advances its timers and stages. Its output service (01E506) sends configuration and purge commands. The two sequences use separate active flags.

    SPEED CONTROL SOFTWARE

    The PCM software contains a speed control function. The switch input is smoothed (02262E, Fig. 6), assigned to one of seven switch classes (02264E), and accepted only after the class is stable (0226B2). Engagement is then qualified against operating conditions and state (0227A2).

    The servo cycle (022E74) updates two request bits, the vacuum and vent requests (02328C). A third control operates the servo supply. The request bits are presented on a shared processor port (01A02A) and released after each pass (01A04A), as described in 5-1 Output Commands. The reverse lockout request uses the same port service (6-3 Reverse Lockout).

    IDLE AIR CONTROL

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    IDLE AIR CONTROL SERVICE

    The PCM adjusts engine idle speed through the idle air control motor. The service manual lists the inputs that affect idle speed: A/C sense, battery voltage, brake switch, coolant temperature, engine speed, engine run time, manifold absolute pressure, throttle position and vehicle speed (Fig. 1).

    The idle air control service (021960) runs on each pass of the fast job schedule. It keeps an idle speed target at F811C and two position counts: the requested position F8612 and the tracked position F8810. Each pass chooses a target and corrects the requested position. When the movement conditions are met, the service hands the difference between the two counts to the companion processor (Fig. 2).

    At the start of each pass the service copies the companion reply byte F8615 to F8629 and reads the pressure compensation F8618 from the curve at ROM 3CDF against pressure value F8804. It then calls the countdown routine (0224E8) and clears F880F bit 08 when F8615 is zero. While the engine-running flag F80D1 bit 40 is set it advances the settle count F8614 by one per pass, holding at FF. While the flag is clear it clears the count. A nonzero speed correction step, a pressure band step that leaves the requested and tracked positions different, and the A/C transition corrections clear the count. The speed correction then waits until the count is above ROM 3962 again.

    IDLE SPEED TARGET

    The target routine (021AC2) stores the idle speed target at F811C as an eighth-rpm word. It builds a target byte and multiplies it by 64, so each count of the target byte is 8 rpm (Fig. 4).

    The target byte comes from the coolant curve at ROM 39B8 (Fig. 3). Calibration option 270B bit 80 is set in this image and selects that curve; the alternate curve at 39A5 holds the same values. The curve gives 124 counts (992 rpm) at -40 °C and below, 112 counts (896 rpm) at 20 °C and 88 counts (704 rpm) at 60 °C and above. Between knots the curve interpolates.

    The runtime curve at ROM 39CB adds to the target byte while the high byte of runtime word F8096 is below FF. The addition is 10 counts (80 rpm) up to a high byte of 4, falls off linearly, and is zero from 10. The sum is limited to FF.

    COOLANTF8096 HIGH BYTETARGET
    60 °C and above0784 rpm
    60 °C and above7744 rpm
    60 °C and above10704 rpm
    20 °C0976 rpm
    −40 °C01072 rpm

    Two flags override the curves. With F8109 bit 80 set, the target byte is the fixed value 100 (800 rpm) and the curves are not read. With F810B bit 02 set, the target byte is raised to at least 64 (512 rpm).

    The service skips the target update while any of F853F bit 08, F880F bit 40, F8128 bit 20 or F8109 bit 40 is set; the previous target stays in F811C. With F8128 bit 80 set it clears the requested position instead and skips to the position handoff. The fuel cut entry and resume tests compare engine speed with this target (3-1 Fuel Amount).

    ENGINE SPEED CORRECTION

    The speed correction (021CD6) runs on a running pass when no earlier branch of the pass has ended it, F80C8 is zero, F80D6 bit 01 is clear and the settle count F8614 is above 63. It forms the difference between engine speed F805A and the target F811C, both eighth-rpm words. Option 270B bit 80 is set in this image, so the routine divides the difference by 8 to give the error in rpm, limited to 255 (Fig. 5).

    The error selects a step from a band table: ROM 39DE when engine speed is below the target, ROM 39F1 when it is at or above. The band routine (022492) does not interpolate. An error at or below the first band edge returns zero; each later edge starts a new band. The positive steps below the target are larger and start closer to the target than the negative steps above it.

    ENGINE SPEEDERROR (RPM)STEP (COUNTS)

    Below target50–93+2
    Below target94–139+3
    Below target140–185+4
    Below target186–231+6
    Below target232–255+8

    A nonzero step is added to the requested position and clears the settle count. The next step therefore waits for the count to pass ROM 3962 again.

    REQUESTED AND TRACKED POSITION

    The corrections described in this section change the requested position F8612. The movement routine changes the tracked position F8810 by the amount it sends. Reset and the recentering routine also write F8810. The difference between the two counts is the movement still to be sent.

    Signed steps reach the requested position through the step routine (02200E). The step is a signed byte. A positive step is limited to the position ceiling 210; a negative step is limited to zero (Fig. 7).

    Position targets from the non-running and off-idle branches go through the slew routine (021B86). Unless F880F bit 04 is set, the routine adds the pressure compensation F8618. It limits the result to ROM 3963. A target above the requested position is applied at once. A target below it lowers the requested position by one count, and only on passes where the low byte of runtime word F8097 masked with FF is zero. With F80D6 bit 40 set the routine clears the bit and applies the target at once, in either direction (Fig. 8).

    NON-RUNNING POSITION TARGET

    When the engine-running flag F80D1 bit 40 is clear, or F880F bit 80 is set, the service sets a position target instead of correcting engine speed. The position target routine (021B50) adds the result of the coolant curve at ROM 3A3E (Fig. 9) to the result of the curve at ROM 3A51 against pressure value F8804, and passes the sum to the slew routine. The routine also clears F880F bit 80 when F880F bit 08 is clear and the companion reply byte F8615 is zero. F8128 bit 08 blocks the routine.

    The reset routine (020000) loads the tracked position F8810 with 223, sets F880F bit 08 and F880F bit 80, and loads FF into F8615. While F880F bit 08 is set the movement routine counts the tracked position down (1-6 Supporting Jobs).

    OFF-IDLE POSITION TARGET

    When the off-idle flag F80D6 bit 80 or F80D6 bit 40 is set, the service calls the off-idle routine (021BCE) in place of the speed correction. The routine forms a base from the coolant curve at ROM 3A64 and the runtime curve at ROM 3A77, and scales it by the curve at ROM 3A8A against pressure value F8804. It takes the largest of that base, the engine speed floor from ROM 3A9D, the throttle floor from ROM 3AB0 against relative throttle F80AC, and the road speed floor from ROM 4084 scaled by ROM 4097. The curve at ROM 4084 holds zero in this image, so the road speed floor is zero. With F810A bit 80 clear and F80D6 bit 40 set it adds 14 counts. The result goes to the slew routine.

    On a pass with F80D6 bit 80 set the service also clears F80D5 bit 02 and skips the pressure control. With only bit 40 set, the pressure control runs after the off-idle routine.

    MANIFOLD PRESSURE CONTROL

    The pressure service (022032) runs on running passes when F80D6 bit 80 is clear. It first builds two manifold pressure values (022146): the target F80A1 and the upper boundary F8625. Engine speed, pressure value F8804 and coolant temperature are normalized through the curves at ROM 3CB9, 3CA6 and 3CCC. With F80D6 bit 01 clear, the grid at ROM 3BAA gives the base of the pressure target (Fig. 11). The grid at ROM 3BFE gives the base of the boundary. To both the routine adds the signed grid at ROM 3C52, read with normalized engine speed and coolant, the runtime curve at ROM 3AD9 and the offset from learned trim F8811. With the A/C clutch request clear, it also adds the engine speed curve at ROM 3D71 and the offset from learned trim F8812. Both values are compared directly with manifold pressure F809B.

    The service then sets the baseline position F8616. The baseline is the grid at ROM 3D05 plus the pressure compensation F8618. With the A/C clutch request (F8107 bit 20) clear and bit 40 of option byte 3961 set, it adds the curve at ROM 3CF2 read with learned trim F8812. Each addition is limited to FF.

    With F80D6 bit 01 set, the service uses the pressure band (0222A0) in place of the speed correction, once the settle count is above 79. Option 3961 bit 80 is clear, which selects the boundary branch (Fig. 10):

    • Manifold pressure at or above boundary F8625 sets F80D5 bit 02. If engine speed is also above the target, the speed correction runs.
    • Manifold pressure below boundary F8625 clears F80D5 bit 02. When manifold pressure is also at or below the target F80A1, the pressure shortfall reads the curve at ROM 3AFF and the result, 0 to +3 counts, goes to the step routine. If the requested and tracked positions then differ, the settle count is cleared.

    The spark advance routine (01015A) tests F80D5 bit 02 (4-1 Spark Timing).

    While F80C8 is nonzero, the service clears F80D5 bit 02 and skips the speed correction, the pressure band, the trim learning and the recentering. The countdown routine (0224E8) clears F80C8 when the road speed byte is below 9 and engine speed is at or below the target, or at higher road speed when manifold pressure is at or below the target F80A1. Otherwise it decrements a nonzero count.

    LEARNED PRESSURE TRIMS

    The PCM keeps two learned pressure trims, one for each state of the A/C clutch request (5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs). The trim routine (022340) adjusts F8811 when F8107 bit 20 is set and F8812 when it is clear; the other trim is left unchanged. Manifold pressure below the target F80A1 lowers the selected trim by one count, stopping at zero. Manifold pressure above the target raises it by one count, stopping at FF. Equal pressure leaves it unchanged. F8880 bit 80 or bit 08 blocks the routine (Fig. 12).

    The target builder reads each trim as a signed offset: the stored value minus 80, divided by 4 and rounded down. The offset ranges from −32 to +31 pressure counts; a stored 80 is no offset. The reset routine writes 80 to both trims, then sets F8812 to 80 again when coolant is below 60 °C.

    The trim routine runs only when all of the following hold on the pass: F80D6 bit 01 is clear and F80C8 is zero; the high bytes of engine speed and target differ by less than 02; the low byte of F8097 masked with 7F is zero; the high byte of F8096 is at or above 1A; coolant is at or above 94 °C; and F8883 bit 80 is clear.

    RECENTERING

    The recentering routine (022398) moves the requested and tracked positions together by one count toward the baseline F8616. It sends no movement, so the difference between the two counts is unchanged (Fig. 13).

    The pressure service calls it when F80D6 bit 01 is clear, F80C8 is zero, the high bytes of engine speed and target differ by less than ROM 3965, the low byte of F8097 masked with ROM 3967 is zero, the settle count is at or above ROM 3962, the requested and tracked positions are equal, the reply byte F8615 is zero, the A/C clutch request is set or option 3961 bit 40 is set, coolant is at or above 86 °C, F8617 is zero, F880F bit 01 is clear, and the requested position differs from the baseline.

    A/C TRANSITION CORRECTIONS

    The A/C clutch control routine (018588) sets and clears F810A bit 40. The A/C transition service (021D28) runs on running passes before the speed correction and compares F810A bit 40 with F810A bit 80. When they differ, it decrements a nonzero delay F8628, or reloads the delay from 0 when it is zero. When the delay is then zero, the service toggles bit 80, applies the first correction (021DA8), sets F810A bit 08 and F85A8 bit 80, and clears the settle count.

    The first correction reads a curve against learned trim F8812 and adds the result through the step routine. With F810A bit 80 set, the curve is ROM 3B38 when F80D6 bit 01 is set and ROM 3B84 when F80D6 bit 01 and bit 80 are clear; at a trim of 80 the step is −7 counts. With F810A bit 80 clear, the curve is ROM 3B12 or ROM 3B5E under the same conditions; at a trim of 80 the step is +7 counts. With F80D6 bit 01 clear and bit 80 set, the step is the road speed curve at ROM 3AC3 scaled by ROM 396C and negated when F810A bit 80 is set; when F810A bit 80 is clear no step is applied. When it applies a step, the routine sets F810A bit 10, and the service skips the off-idle and speed correction branches on that pass.

    The correction also loads the hold count F8613: 27 with bit 80 set, 28 with bit 80 clear. When a step is applied, the size of the step, scaled by BA, is added, limited to FF. While the bits agree and the hold count is nonzero, each pass clears the settle count and decrements the hold. When the hold is zero with F810A bit 08 set, the follow-up correction (021E7C) runs once from curves 3B25, 3B4B, 3B71 or 3B97 and F810A bit 08 is cleared. The follow-up curves hold zero in this image.

    POSITION HANDOFF

    At the end of each pass the service calls the movement routine (0223B6) when the supply value F816E is at or above 7A and engine speed is at or below 8000 rpm. The routine requires F8171 bit 01 set and fewer than 9 commands waiting in the queue (F80E4). Each command carries at most 1F counts. While F8847 bit 80 is set the limit is 3 counts, and the routine sends nothing while F8615 is nonzero. The routine moves the tracked position toward the requested position by the amount sent before it queues the command.

    The queue routine (022432) marks F8615 pending (FF) and queues command 22, select 1E. While F8615 is nonzero, each pass queues status poll command 36, select 1E, with the reply returned into F8615 (022452). The command format and the reset mode are described in 1-6 Supporting Jobs.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    DRB IDLE AIR TESTS

    Each DRB idle air test writes the requested position F8612. The movement routine sends the difference between F8612 and the tracked position F8810 in the same way as for idle control.

    SR6 · SPEED AND TRANSMISSION6 - 1

    VEHICLE SPEED INPUT

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    VEHICLE SPEED SENSOR

    The vehicle speed sensor is located on the driver's side of the transmission (Fig. 1). The PCM determines vehicle speed from the speed sensor input.

    The sensor signal travels on circuit G7 from sensor terminal 3 through connectors C330 and C111 to PCM cavity C2-28. The PCM supplies 5 volts to sensor terminal 1 on circuit K6 from cavity C2-31, and provides the sensor ground on circuit K4 at cavity C3-4 (Fig. 2). Circuit G17 at cavity C2-27 is the speedometer signal, a separate circuit; it is not the speed sensor input.

    PULSE CAPTURE

    Each speed sensor edge is recorded by timer input-capture channel 2. The timer service inside the periodic interrupt (028502) reads the captured 16-bit time and extends it with a software overflow count at F8052. When a timer overflow falls close to the captured edge, the service corrects the overflow count so that the edge and the overflow are counted in the right order (Fig. 3).

    The service subtracts the previous 32-bit timestamp from the new one. The difference is the pulse period, stored at F8084–F8087. The new timestamp replaces the previous one, the new-sample flag (F80CB, bit 80) sets, and the sample counter at F80A3 reloads to 41. A shorter period means a higher vehicle speed.

    SPEED CALCULATION

    The vehicle speed service (01E14E) calculates a new speed only when the new-sample flag is set, and clears the flag as it starts (Fig. 4). The same routine also handles serial and distance-counter work.

    Averaging. When the previous speed byte is at or above 60, the service adds each period to a running sum and counts the periods. Until the eighth period arrives, the service saves the sum and leaves the speed unchanged. On the eighth period it divides the sum by eight, clears the sum and the count, and continues with the average. Below that speed every period is used directly.

    Division. The V10 application (configuration byte 02) selects the reciprocal constant at ROM 045E–0461; the alternate application uses the constant at ROM 045A–045D. The service shifts the constant and the period right together until the period fits in 16 bits, divides, and rounds the quotient to the nearest count. The result is the speed target (Fig. 5).

    Filtering. The target feeds two filtered speed words through the filter routine (029D16). Each pass moves the word toward the target by a calibrated fraction of the difference and keeps the remainder in a fractional byte, so small changes accumulate. The road-speed word at F8135 uses 24/256 when rising and 24/256 when falling. The second word at F8648 uses 64/256 and 64/256.

    Speed byte. The service forms the vehicle speed byte at F80A4 from the road-speed word by discarding its five low bits. When bit 13 of the word is set, the byte is set to FF (Fig. 6).

    SAMPLE EXPIRY

    The fast watchdog service (01FCBC) calls the speed expiry routine (01E114) on each pass. Each call with a nonzero sample counter decrements the counter and returns. A call that finds the counter already at zero clears the speed byte, both filtered speed words and flag F80D6 bit 01 (Fig. 7).

    On the V10 application the expiry also sets the stored period to FFFFFFFF, sets flag F80CA bit 10 and clears bits C0 of timer control register TCTL1. Every captured pulse reloads the counter, so a steady pulse train holds the speed reading. Starting from a fresh reload, the speed clears on the 42nd pass without a new pulse.

    SPEED USERS

    The vehicle speed byte and the road-speed word are shared by several controls. When the speed expires, each user sees zero speed on its next evaluation.

    • Reverse lockout (024ADE) sets its request only while the speed byte is greater than 6; a zero speed clears the request. Refer to 6-3 Reverse Lockout.
    • Skip shift (0249F4) compares the speed byte with its calibrated speed windows. Refer to 6-2 Transmission Controls.
    • The engine-to-road speed ratio (029CBC) divides engine speed by the road-speed word scaled down by eight; a zero scaled word sets the filtered ratio word at F8133 to FFFF. Refer to 6-2 Transmission Controls.
    • The scan tool vehicle speed (OBD PID 0D) in 01E5E6 reports the speed byte × 206 ÷ 256, rounded, in km/h.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    VEHICLE SPEED SENSOR CIRCUIT

    The PCM sets trouble code 15 (P0500) when no vehicle speed sensor signal is detected during road load conditions (Fig. 8).

    The signal, 5-volt supply and ground circuits are listed under Specifications.

    NOTE: When no new speed pulse is captured, the speed reading clears once the sample counter expires and the scan tool reports zero speed. Each new pulse reloads the counter and the calculation resumes.

    TRANSMISSION CONTROLS

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    TRANSMISSION CONTROL DISPATCH

    The Viper uses a six-speed manual transmission with two PCM-controlled solenoids: the skip shift solenoid and the reverse lockout solenoid, both on the transmission case beside the vehicle speed sensor (6-1, Fig. 1). The PCM software that serves them is part of a program shared with automatic-transmission applications. A configuration byte selects which body of transmission software runs.

    The transmission control dispatcher (023430) first calls the shift torque routine (024AF4), then stores whole engine speed at F805C, computed as the engine-speed word shifted right three places. It then tests bit 02 of the engine selector at ROM 2707. In this calibration the selector reads 02, so the dispatcher calls the skip shift controller (0249F4), jumps to the reverse lockout request (024ADE) and returns (Fig. 1). The automatic-transmission body that begins at 023450 is not entered. Reverse lockout is described in 6-3 Reverse Lockout.

    SKIP SHIFT CONTROL

    The skip shift solenoid prevents the driver from shifting into second or third gear while its lockout conditions are met; the shift indicator lamp tells the driver to shift into fourth gear on the next upshift. The PCM controls the solenoid on circuit K33 at PCM cavity C1-6 and the first-to-fourth shift indicator lamp on circuit G54 at cavity C2-11 (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).

    The skip shift controller (0249F4) writes two request bits in the discrete output byte F8107. Bit 08 is the solenoid request and bit 80 is the lamp request. Both are active when clear. At startup the byte is loaded from ROM 3DAF, which reads FF, so both requests start inactive. The controller compares the vehicle speed byte F80A4, coolant F80A6, the engine-speed word F805A, the engine-to-road speed ratio F8133 and relative throttle F80AC with the thirteen calibration bytes at ROM 3DA0 through 3DAC (Fig. 2).

    Re-arm. Below the re-arm speed at ROM 3DA0 the controller clears its attempt and inhibit flags (F814D bits 80 and 01) and reloads the ratio wait counter from ROM 3DAA. An active solenoid request stays active through this branch.

    Entry conditions. On a new attempt the controller requires coolant at or above ROM 3DA1, engine speed at or above the word at ROM 3DAB, vehicle speed inside the window set by ROM 3DA8 and ROM 3DA7, an engine-to-road speed ratio inside the window set by ROM 3DA2 and ROM 3DA6, and relative throttle below ROM 3DA3. When every condition passes, the controller sets the attempt flag. If the inhibit flag is clear, it then clears bits 08 and 80 of F8107 to request the solenoid and the lamp, and loads the release hold counter F8416 from ROM 3DA9. The attempt flag is set before the inhibit flag is tested, so each low-speed cycle makes one attempt only.

    Hold and release. While conditions remain in the window, the requests stay on. Coolant or engine speed below its limit, or vehicle speed below ROM 3DA4, sends the controller to its release path: each pass decrements the hold counter while the solenoid request is active, and at zero sets bit 08 and then bit 80. A ratio at or above ROM 3DA6 counts down the ratio wait counter and cancels when it reaches zero. With the ratio below ROM 3DA6, vehicle speed at or above ROM 3DA7, or throttle at or above ROM 3DA3, cancels at once: the hold counter clears, the inhibit flag sets, and the release path ends the request on the same pass. A ratio below ROM 3DA2 sets the inhibit flag and enters the release path with the hold counter intact. Vehicle speed between ROM 3DA4 and ROM 3DA8 leaves both requests unchanged. The request and release instructions are shown in Fig. 5.

    ENGINE-TO-ROAD SPEED RATIO

    The controller identifies first gear from the ratio of engine speed to road speed. The ratio service (029CBC) averages the current and previous engine-speed words, divides the result by the filtered vehicle-speed word F8135 scaled down by eight, and limits the quotient to FF. The sample is then smoothed by the 8-bit filter (029F70), using a rising factor of DA and a falling factor of DA. The filtered ratio is stored at F8133. When the scaled road speed is zero, the service writes FFFF to F8133, which places the ratio above the skip shift window (Fig. 6).

    OUTPUT HANDLING

    The changed-output service (029AFC) compares F8107 with the last queued byte at F8104 and queues a new command only when the byte has changed and the command queue has room. When F811F bit 02 is clear, the service masks the byte with the startup mask at ROM 270F, which reads 90. The mask clears bits 80 and 10 of the queued byte; bit 08, the solenoid request, passes unchanged. Refer to 5-1 Output Commands for the command queue.

    SHARED AUTOMATIC TRANSMISSION STRUCTURES

    Calibration regions 9000 and A000 hold the shared automatic-transmission structures: output-shaft speed and gear estimation (0238BE), governor pressure regulation (023D3E), torque converter clutch boundaries (02460C) and a 17 × 9 interpolation grid. The Viper branch of the dispatcher bypasses these control routines. They are listed in 9-4 Transmission Tables.

    Seven automatic-transmission monitors are dispatched by the configured monitor service (019194). Each has a configuration record whose bit 01 enables it. In this calibration bit 01 is clear in all seven records, so the service marks each monitor state disabled and skips its handler.

    The shift torque routine (024AF4) computes a spark retard value at F8457, which the spark routine subtracts from advance (4-1 Spark Timing). The routine runs only when ROM A009 bit 40 is set. A009 reads 00, so the routine branches to its exit at its first instruction.

    REVERSE LOCKOUT

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    REVERSE LOCKOUT SOLENOID

    The reverse lockout solenoid prevents the driver from shifting the T-56 transmission into reverse above a low vehicle speed. Power for the solenoid is supplied on circuit F12 from fuse 10 (10 A), which is hot with the ignition switch in START or RUN. The PCM controls the ground side of the coil on circuit K136 at PCM cavity C2-21 (Fig. 1). When the PCM provides the ground, the solenoid energizes and allows shifting into reverse; when the ground is removed, the solenoid de-energizes and the transmission cannot be shifted into reverse.

    The solenoid is mounted on the transmission case, which also carries the skip shift solenoid and the vehicle speed sensor (6-1, Fig. 1). The skip shift solenoid is served by a separate controller and a separate output path (6-2 Transmission Controls).

    REVERSE LOCKOUT REQUEST

    The reverse lockout request is decided once per pass of the transmission control dispatcher (023430). With the engine selector at ROM 2707 reading 02, the dispatcher runs the skip shift controller and then jumps to the reverse lockout request routine (024ADE). The request path from the filtered speed word to the processor port is shown in Fig. 3.

    The routine is seven instructions long (Fig. 2). It loads the vehicle speed byte F80A4, compares it with the calibration byte at ROM 3DAD, which reads 06, and writes bit 20 of the request byte F8502:

    • Speed byte greater than 06 (07 and above): bit 20 is set.
    • Speed byte 06 or less: bit 20 is cleared.

    The comparison is unsigned and strict. One threshold serves both directions: the routine has no separate release value, no timer and no debounce, and it rewrites the bit on every pass regardless of its previous state. All other bits of F8502 are preserved.

    VEHICLE SPEED BYTE

    The speed byte F80A4 is produced by the vehicle speed service (01E14E) from the filtered road-speed word F8135 by discarding its five low bits; across the normal speed range the byte is the word divided by 32, rounded down. Filtered word 223 gives byte 06 and leaves the request clear; word 224 gives byte 07 and sets it. The road-speed word is smoothed by the shared filter (029D16) with a factor of 18 rising and 18 falling, so the same smoothing applies whether the vehicle is speeding up or slowing down. The scan tool reports the speed byte as byte × 206 ÷ 256 km/h, rounded to the nearest whole km/h: byte 06 reads 5 km/h and byte 07 reads 6 km/h (Fig. 4). Refer to 6-1 Vehicle Speed Input for speed capture and filtering.

    OUTPUT PORT

    The reverse lockout request does not pass through the output command queue used by the skip shift solenoid. The fast vehicle-state job (01FC58) presents it directly on a processor port. The drive service (01A02A) copies bits 08, 10, 20 and 40 of F8502 into the port GP data register without inversion, keeps the register's other bits, and sets the same four bits of the port GP direction register so the pins drive as outputs (Fig. 5). Later in the same job, the release service (01A04A) clears those four direction bits and returns the pins to inputs. The shared port and its read-back checks are described in 5-1 Output Commands.

    The speed control servo service (02328C) shares F8502 and writes only bits 08 and 10, so the reverse lockout request in bit 20 passes through it unchanged (5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs).

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    DRB REVERSE LOCKOUT TEST

    The DRB reverse lockout solenoid test (00EB74) operates the same request bit as normal control, F8502 bit 20, so the test exercises the same port path. The test runs only when bit 02 of the engine selector at ROM 2707 is set. With bit 08 of the test state flags at F8128 clear, it sets bit 20. With bit 08 set and bit 01 clear, it reverses the current state of bit 20 each time it runs.

    SPEED BYTE F80A4F8502 BIT 20SCAN TOOL
    00–06Clear0–5 km/h
    07 and aboveSet6 km/h and above

    A filtered speed that moves back and forth between words 223 and 224 changes the request on each pass, because the routine uses one threshold in both directions.

    SR7 · SENSOR FAULT HANDLING7 - 1

    SUBSTITUTE VALUES

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    INPUT RANGE CHECKS

    Before the PCM uses a throttle position, coolant temperature, intake air temperature or manifold pressure reading, it compares the raw converter value with a calibrated low and high limit (Fig. 1). Each sensor has its own check routine: throttle position (019BDC), coolant temperature (019C06), intake air temperature (019CDC) and manifold pressure (019D06). The limits are inclusive. A reading below the low limit or above the high limit sets the sensor's immediate-invalid bit in F811F; a reading inside the limits clears it. Refer to Specifications.

    Each check returns a result code to its caller: 08 for a low reading, 84 for a high reading and 44 for a reading inside the limits. The immediate-invalid bit is separate from the stored trouble code and from the active fault flags that select a substitute (7-2 Sensor Recovery).

    The manifold pressure check runs only inside an operating window. Engine speed must be between 416 rpm and 3520 rpm, and relative throttle opening F80AC must not exceed 3A. Outside the window the routine returns 00 and leaves the previous manifold pressure invalid bit unchanged (Fig. 2). A skipped check is not a passed check.

    INPUT SELECTION

    The throttle, coolant temperature and intake air temperature services follow the same order of decisions (Fig. 3). An active fault flag in F8808 or F8809 selects the substitute value first. Without an active fault flag, an immediate-invalid sample holds the last working value. Only a sample that passes the range check is converted and updates the working value. A rejected temperature or throttle sample never becomes the working value; the held value stays in use until a valid sample or the substitute replaces it.

    The intake air temperature service (01F8BC) copies F8353 into working value F80A5 when fault flag F8808 bit 08 is set. When immediate-invalid bit F811F.08 is set it returns without changing F80A5. Otherwise it converts the reading through the thermistor conversion curve (Fig. 4) and moves F80A5 toward the result by no more than 9 counts per pass.

    The coolant temperature service (01F926) transfers to the coolant fallback when fault flag F8808 bit 80 is set. Otherwise it clears fallback latch F8495 bit 04. With immediate-invalid bit F811F.10 set it returns before updating working value F80A6; with a valid sample it converts the reading through the same thermistor curve, limits the step to 9 counts and then updates the derived coolant value F80A2 through curve 266F.

    The throttle service (0297D0) copies the raw throttle byte F8036 into working throttle F80AD only when immediate-invalid bit F811F.20 is clear. Its substitute is described below.

    THROTTLE, INTAKE AIR AND MANIFOLD PRESSURE SUBSTITUTES

    The PCM substitutes for an incorrect signal with values from other sensors and from calibration (Fig. 5).

    Throttle position. When fault flag F8808 bit 10 or F8809 bit 08 is set, the throttle service resets learned closed-throttle reference F8803 to 28 and writes the same value to working throttle F80AD. When pressure byte F809B is at or above D2, the working throttle substitute is raised by the larger-opening margin 7D plus one, limited to FF (Fig. 6). The throttle substitute therefore depends on the manifold pressure reading.

    Intake air temperature. The substitute is F8353. The external status poll (014136) fills F8353 by queuing command 2C with select 1E, or loads the calibrated value 32 °C when flag F848F bit 20 is set.

    Manifold pressure. The manifold pressure converter (029A56) uses the estimate routine (029A96) in place of the sensor when any of fault flags F8808 bit 20, F8809 bit 20 or F8808 bit 40 is set, or when immediate-invalid bit F811F.04 is set after the range check (019D06). A caller that sets F811F bit 01 around the call gets the scaling step alone: the converter skips the fault flags, the range check and the estimate. The value supplied by the caller and the estimate leave through the same scaling step.

    The estimate is built from engine speed, working throttle F80AD and learned reference F8803. Below 3200 rpm, engine speed above 800 rpm is multiplied by 3A; the rounded high byte of the product plus the learned reference is subtracted from working throttle plus 11. A negative result, or engine speed at or above the upper limit, gives an index of zero. The index addresses curve 600F, and the curve output plus 0D, limited to FF, is the estimate. Because the estimate uses working throttle, a throttle fault and a manifold pressure fault together produce an estimate from the throttle substitute.

    COOLANT TEMPERATURE SUBSTITUTE

    The coolant fallback (01F99A) runs in place of the normal coolant conversion while fault flag F8808 bit 80 is set (Fig. 7). It builds the substitute from the intake air temperature, from F8353, or from a calibrated warm value, depending on engine state.

    With the engine not running (F80D1 bit 40 clear), working coolant F80A6 takes the working intake air temperature F80A5. When intake air temperature is itself invalid or faulted, F80A6 takes F8353 instead.

    On the first pass with the engine running, the routine sets latch F8495 bit 04 and seeds F80A6 once. When the high byte of runtime word F8096 is below 40, the seed is the intake air value selected as above. At or above that age, the seed is the calibrated target 40 °C.

    On later running passes the routine compares phase bit F8493 bit 08 with bit 80 of F8097. When they differ and the phase bit is clear, the routine sets the phase bit and leaves the temperature unchanged. When they differ and the phase bit is set, it clears the phase bit and moves F80A6 one count toward the calibrated target. The substitute therefore moves one count per two phase changes and stops at the target. Every exit of the fallback updates the derived coolant value F80A2 through curve 266F.

    SPEED INPUT EXPIRY

    Vehicle speed uses a sample counter rather than a range check. When no new speed sample reloads the counter, the expiry routine (01E114) clears the speed byte and both filtered speed words. Consumers of these values then read zero, including the reverse lockout request (024ADE) and the engine-to-road speed ratio (029CBC). Refer to 6-1 Vehicle Speed Input and 6-3 Reverse Lockout.

    7 - 27 · SENSOR FAULT HANDLINGSR

    SENSOR RECOVERY

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    SIMPLE SENSOR CHECKS

    The PCM tests its basic sensor inputs through a common dispatcher, the simple diagnostic check service (019060). The dispatcher walks three parallel tables of 24 records each: the check routines at ROM C0D6, the configuration records at ROM 70E2 and the qualification policy records at ROM 1003. A configuration record whose bit 01 is clear is skipped.

    Fault IDs in this section are written in hexadecimal, as in the service manual trouble code charts. The configuration table lists the same IDs in decimal.

    Each check routine returns a result category. The MAP, intake air temperature, coolant and throttle position checks reach the range checks 019D06, 019CDC, 019C06 and 019BDC. A failing result sends the high-side or low-side fault ID from the configuration record to the failure qualifier. A passing result sends a fault ID to the recovery counter. The range checks also set and clear immediate-invalid flags in F811F; those flags are separate from the qualified fault state described below (7-1 Substitute Values).

    FAILURE QUALIFICATION

    A failing result does not change the input source immediately. The failure qualifier (018D28) counts accepted failure observations against the failure threshold in byte 2 of the policy record (Fig. 2). For the fault IDs in this section, an observation is accepted only when the sensor supply reading F816E is at or above A8 (ROM 120A) and the inhibit flags F80CA.02 and F8492.40 are clear.

    The qualifier holds its counts in two shared slots, F8163/F8164 and F8165/F8166. Each slot holds one fault ID and its count. A matching ID increments its slot; a new ID takes a vacant slot with a count of 1. When both slots hold other IDs, the observation is not counted. Good readings do not reset a slot. Instead, the qualified countdown service (01F660) lowers both counts by one on each visit and releases a slot whose count reaches zero. A sensor that fails intermittently therefore qualifies only when its failures outpace this decay.

    When the count reaches the threshold, the qualifier stores the fault ID in F8475 and F887A, empties its slot and selects the recording path named by the configuration byte. The four sensor checks use configuration B9, which selects the forced-record path (0150B6) ahead of the fault record service (0150F8).

    STORED CODE AND ACTIVE FALLBACK

    A qualified failure produces two separate pieces of state. The fault record service adds the fault ID to the stored-code bitmap at F8848 and to the report-order list at F8868, which holds eight IDs with the newest first (8-2 Fault Reporting). Its tail calls the active-fault service (018E18), which uses byte 0 of the policy record to set one active fallback flag in F8808: the low nibble selects the bit and bits 4–6 select the byte.

    The input routines read the active fallback flag, not the stored code, when they choose between the sensor and a substitute value (7-1 Substitute Values). The service manual describes this condition as limp-in mode (7-1, Fig. 5).

    RECOVERY OF THE ACTIVE FLAG

    Passing results reach the recovery counter (019112), which acts only while the check's active fallback flag is set. The dispatcher tests the high-side pass category first, so recovery always counts under the high-side fault ID. A coolant fault stored as low-side ID 1E recovers under ID 1F; a MAP fault stored as ID 24 recovers under ID 25.

    One shared word, F84B6, holds the recovering fault ID and its clear count for all checks. The counter advances when the word is empty or already holds the same ID; a passing result under a different ID leaves the word unchanged and is not counted. When the count reaches the clear threshold in byte 1 of the policy record, the routine empties the word and clears the active flag (Fig. 5). It does not touch the stored-code bitmap or the report-order list, so the code remains stored after the PCM returns to the sensor.

    Three events interrupt recovery. A failure observation with the same ID as the pending recovery empties the word, so a high-side failure resets coolant recovery while a low-side failure leaves it in place. The fault record service empties the word when it records that ID. The countdown service lowers the clear count by one, but only on a visit that leaves the second failure slot at zero.

    The configuration byte selects the clear method. With bit 20 set, as in configuration B9, the counted path applies. With bit 20 clear and bit 08 set, the first passing result clears the active flag.

    Startup also clears active flags. After the retained memory check (1-2 Startup and Initialization), the reset routine walks the 24 configuration records and, for each record with bit 10 set and bit 08 clear, calls 019396, which clears the active flag named by byte 0 of the policy record (Fig. 6). Among the enabled checks only the charging voltage check qualifies: configuration 31, fault ID 06, active flag F880A.40 from policy byte 27. The four sensor checks and the P1296 check have bit 08 set, so their active flags stay set across a reset whenever the retained area is kept. The reset applies the same rule to the configured-monitor records at 712D.

    RETURN TO NORMAL INPUT

    Coolant. The coolant filter (01F926) runs the range check and then tests F8808.80. While the flag is set, it uses the coolant fallback (01F99A). Once the flag clears, it clears the fallback-entry latch F8495.04. While the immediate-invalid flag F811F.10 is clear, it converts the sample and moves the working coolant value F80A6 toward the converted value by no more than 9 counts per visit. The working value therefore returns to the sensor reading gradually.

    MAP. The MAP converter (029A56) uses the substitute pressure while any of three active flags is set: F8808.20 for the basic input codes, F8808.40 for P1296 and F8809.20 for P1297. It also uses the substitute while the immediate-invalid flag F811F.04 is set after the range check. Clearing the basic MAP flag restores the sensor only when the other two flags are also clear (Fig. 7). Override bit F811F.01 bypasses all four tests.

    The P1296 check (019D4C) uses configuration 99, so its active flag clears on the first passing result. The check passes while latch F8802.80 is clear; with the latch set, it fails until the MAP reading high byte reaches 78, then clears the latch and passes. The MAP-response monitor (01A810) behind P1297 keeps its own pass and failure counters F8477/F8476 and compares them with 20 and 20. After the monitor qualifies a clear result, the shared recovery counter clears F8809.20 at a threshold of 1.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    STORED CODES AFTER RECOVERY

    Recovery leaves the stored-code bitmap and the report-order list unchanged, so a code stays stored after the sensor has returned to normal. The active fallback flag and the stored code clear by separate paths, so a stored code does not show that the PCM is still using a substitute value. Stored codes and their reporting are described in 8-2 Fault Reporting.

    The first column of the service manual trouble code charts lists the fault ID in hexadecimal. These are the same IDs the PCM stores in its configuration records, its qualification slots and its recovery word (Fig. 8, Fig. 9, Fig. 10, Fig. 11).

    SR8 · ON-BOARD DIAGNOSTICS8 - 1

    DIAGNOSTIC OVERVIEW

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    DIAGNOSTIC SYSTEM

    The PCM watches its sensor inputs, output circuits and control results, and stores a trouble code when a fault qualifies (Fig. 2). The software divides this work into four parts: monitors that make observations, result services that qualify them, a stored-fault record, and the services that report stored faults (Fig. 1).

    Three families of monitors make the observations. Each family has its own dispatch table and its own enable settings. A monitor reports a passing or a failing result. The result services decide whether a failing result is recorded as a fault, and whether a passing result releases an active fault (8-2 Fault Reporting).

    A recorded fault is held by its internal fault identifier. Three services report the fault state: the indicator request, the two-digit blink display (8-3 Blink Code Display), and the scan tool service on the SCI link.

    MONITOR FAMILIES

    Detailed monitors. The detailed monitor service (0147F0) runs in the fast job group through 01FCBC (1-5 Scheduled Jobs). It walks thirteen 14-byte descriptors from C020 (Fig. 4). Each descriptor names a callback routine, a fault-id list, a state byte in RAM, a configuration record and three condition lists; the service reads the first two lists itself (8-2 Fault Reporting). A descriptor runs only when its bit in the enable mask at ROM 6F2A is set. The first descriptor tests bit 1000 and each following descriptor tests the next lower bit (Fig. 3).

    The reference image holds 0800 in the mask, so descriptor C02E is the one detailed monitor in service. Its callback is the fuel system monitor (01C512), which compares fuel trim against rich and lean limits and reports P0172, P0171, P0175 and P0174 (3-2 Fuel Feedback). A descriptor is also skipped when its state byte has bit 80 set, or when its configuration cadence bits overlap the runtime counter byte at F8097.

    The condition lists are read by a shared interpreter (01497A); their format and use are described in 8-2 Fault Reporting. When the callback returns, state bit 20 sends the result to the passing-result service (0149DE) and state bit 10 sends it to the failing-result service (014A94).

    Simple checks. The simple-check service (019060) walks 24 routine slots from C0D6 alongside 24 configuration triples from 70E2. Bit 01 of the first configuration byte enables the slot. The second and third bytes are the high-side and low-side fault identifiers. The check returns its result in register A: bit 80 reports a high-side failure and bit 08 a low-side failure, each passed to 018D28; bits 40 and 04 report passes, passed to 019112 when configuration bit 10 is set. Ten slots are enabled in the reference image (refer to Specifications).

    Configured monitors. The configured-monitor service (019194) walks thirty 12-byte descriptors from C106. A two-byte record at 712D accompanies each descriptor: bit 01 of the first byte enables normal dispatch and the second byte is the fault identifier. The simple checks and the configured monitors are both visited by 018BB6 after it processes the queued external fault observations. It runs in the medium job group through 0138AA, and divides its local work by the count at ROM 1219, 4.

    TROUBLE CODE RECORDS

    Every reportable fault has a three-byte record in the diagnostic-code catalog at ROM 1222 (8-2, Fig. 4, 8-2 Fault Reporting). The record for fault identifier n is at 1222 + 3 × n. The first two bytes hold the generic scan tool code and the third byte holds the two-digit MIL code. A record with a zero word carries no generic code.

    The fault identifier, written in hexadecimal, is the HEX CODE column of the trouble code chart in the service manual (Fig. 5). Identifier 01 reads P0340 and MIL code 54, identifier 02 reads P0601 and 53, and identifiers 05 and 06 carry MIL codes 47 and 46 with no generic code, exactly as charted. Two records can share a MIL code: identifiers 99 and 9A (P1493 and P1492) both carry 44.

    The record service (0150F8) stores the identifier in the stored-fault bitmap at F8848 and in the report-order list at F8868. Fault storage and the catalog are described in 8-2 Fault Reporting.

    INDICATOR REQUEST

    The indicator service (015054) runs on every visit of the detailed-monitor service and sets the indicator request, F8107 bit 10, from the fault-state flags at F8886 (8-2, Fig. 5). The request policy is described in 8-2 Fault Reporting. While the blink display is active (F8886 bit 04), the service leaves the request to the blink serializer and cancels the display on the conditions described in 8-3 Blink Code Display.

    SCAN TOOL COMMUNICATION

    The DRB scan tool communicates with the PCM over the SCI link, circuits D20 and D21 at PCM cavities C1-29 and C1-27. Received bytes are handled by the SCI diagnostic service (00C800). Command bytes 10 through 30 are accepted. Each command has a flag byte in the table at ECC2 that names the argument bytes that follow, and the arguments are stored at F8346, F8347 and F8348. Every accepted byte is echoed through the transmit routine (00EBC0). When the last argument arrives, the service sets F8128 bit 01 and jumps to the handler selected from the table at ECE2, which holds the handlers for commands 10 through 2F (Fig. 6, Fig. 7).

    Command 13 runs a circuit actuation test: its argument indexes the actuator-test table at F0DE, and each test operates the same request that normal control uses (5-2 Accessory and Evaporative Outputs). Command 14 returns a report value selected from the report table at F17C. Command 26 reads one byte of flash (banks 00 to 03) or of RAM from F8000 to F8A04. Command 28 reads one of 512 logical EEPROM locations through the address map at 0934. Command 2A returns identification bytes. Commands 15, 16 and 1C to 20 complete with no further reply.

    Generic scan tool requests are answered by 01E5E6 in the fast job group. For mode 01 it reads the parameter number at F8347 and returns the matching value, among them coolant temperature, fuel trim for each bank, MAP, engine speed, vehicle speed, spark advance, intake air temperature and throttle position.

    A diagnostic session ends on timeout. The timeout service (01F2E2) clears the request state at F8345 to F834C, resets the SCI registers and restores the outputs that an actuator test had taken over.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    READING TROUBLE CODES

    Stored codes are displayed by the DRB scan tool or by the MIL blink display (Fig. 8). The DRB reads codes over the SCI link. The blink display translates each stored identifier through the third byte of its catalog record (8-3 Blink Code Display).
