    8 - 28 · ON-BOARD DIAGNOSTICSSR

    FAULT REPORTING

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    MONITOR FAMILIES

    The PCM software tests its circuits and systems through three families of monitors. Each family has its own table of callbacks, its own enable settings and its own working memory. A monitor that is present in a table runs only when its enable bit and its operating conditions allow it. The service manual describes the same principle: a fault is recorded only when the criteria for the check are met (8-1 Diagnostic Overview).

    The tables, enable settings and dispatch of the three monitor families are described in 8-1 Diagnostic Overview. In the reference calibration one of the thirteen detailed monitors (0147F0) is enabled: descriptor C02E, the rich/lean fuel correction monitor (01C512, 3-2 Fuel Feedback). Ten of the twenty-four simple checks (019060) are enabled; the first four are the MAP, intake air temperature, coolant temperature and throttle position range checks (7-2 Sensor Recovery). Eleven of the thirty configured monitors (019194) are enabled (Fig. 7).

    CONDITION LISTS

    Every descriptor points to condition lists in ROM. A list is a count followed by four-byte entries: a working-memory address, an operator and a byte operand. The condition-list evaluator (01497A) accepts only addresses inside working memory F8000–F8A04 and recognizes four operators: mask nonzero, mask zero, value at or above the operand, and value below the operand. The list matches when any one of its entries matches. A list with a count of zero is skipped.

    The detailed service evaluates the first list only while F8886 bit 80 (set by a forced record) is set; a match sets bit 80 of the monitor state byte, and the service then passes over that descriptor. The second list sets a shared condition flag (F8886, bit 20) before the service calls the monitor. The failure-record gate (01525A) evaluates a third descriptor list and sets or clears the record-inhibit flag (F8886, bit 10) that the qualification routines read.

    FROM RESULT TO FAULT RECORD

    A monitor reports what it observed on one visit. After the callback returns, the detailed service reads the monitor state byte: bit 20 routes a clear result to the clear handler (0149DE), bit 10 routes a failure result to the failure handler (014A94) (8-1, Fig. 3). The result-mask translator (0151D2) takes the lowest set bit of the result word F8157, selects the matching entry of the descriptor's id list and places it in the working fault id F8475. For the fuel correction monitor the id list at ROM 6DDE holds four ids, one for each bank and direction.

    The failure handler applies the policy that the descriptor selects (Fig. 2):

    • History (014E62) uses packed history nibbles at F8902–F8981, first-failure and past-failure flags and a once-per-visit guard. It records the fault and requests a freeze-record capture.
    • Staged (014DB8) holds a pending bit from one eligible stage and records the fault at a later eligible stage.
    • Forced (0150B6) sets the selected nibble to its qualified state, sets F8886 bit 80 and records the fault at once.
    • Direct records the fault through the recording service without a history stage.

    A clear result advances the retest history (014F98). While F887A holds a fault id, the clear handler also releases the freeze record when its saved rank is below 3 and its saved id matches the fault that passed. It does not erase the stored fault. The freeze record, its replacement rule and the aging of stored faults are described in 8-5 Fault Snapshot and History.

    The simple checks use their own pair of services. Result bits 80 and 08 send the high or low fault id to the observation accumulator (018D28), which counts failures in two shared id/count slots at F8163 and F8165 before it selects the configured record path. A divided timer decays these counts. Result bits 40 and 04 send a clear observation to the recovery service (019112) when configuration bit 10 is set. That service clears only the active-fallback bit in F8808, at once or after a count of passing visits as the check's configuration selects; the stored fault record stays in place. Substitute values and their recovery are described in 7-1 Substitute Values and 7-2 Sensor Recovery.

    FAULT STORAGE

    The recording service (0150F8) stores the working fault id in two places (Fig. 3):

    • Stored-fault bitmap. Thirty-two bytes at F8848–F8867 hold one bit for each of 256 internal ids. The byte index is the id divided by eight; the bit is the id's low three bits.
    • Report-order list. Eight bytes at F8868 hold the most recent distinct ids. An id already in the list ends the recording there: the list and the bitmap are left as they are. A new id enters the first position, the earlier ids move down one place and the eighth is dropped.

    An id of zero is not recorded. When the record comes from a simple or configured check whose configuration has bit 10 set, the service also activates that check's fallback flag (018E18). The stored-bit query (01F406) reads one id back from the bitmap using the same index and mask.

    CODE CATALOG

    Internal fault ids translate to reportable codes through the diagnostic-code catalog at ROM 1222. The catalog holds 240 three-byte records, indexed by internal id. The first two bytes are the OBD code word in decimal digits (for example 0172 for P0172); the third byte is the two-digit legacy blink code. A record with a zero code word has a blink code only. The OBD request service (01E5E6) and the blink-code serializer (013EF4) read the same records, so the DRB display and the lamp display of one fault come from one catalog entry (8-3 Blink Code Display).

    The internal id is the value printed in the HEX CODE column of the service manual trouble code charts (8-1, Fig. 5). Hex code 01 is catalog record 1 (P0340, blink 54); hex codes 76–79 are the four fuel correction ids at ROM 6DDE (P0172, P0171, P0175, P0174). Every generic code and every MIL code printed in the charts matches the catalog record of its hex code. Several ids share one blink code, as the charts show for the injector and oxygen sensor groups.

    INDICATOR REQUEST

    The indicator service (015054) runs at the end of every detailed-monitor pass and directly whenever blink mode is active. It owns the malfunction indicator request, F8107 bit 10 (Fig. 5). While blink mode is active, the service returns without change unless the capture flag (F80CE, bit 10) or the diagnostic flag (F8109, bit 01) is set; either flag cancels blink mode and clears its count, progress, list index and working id. In normal operation the flags in F8886 decide the request. With bit 40 set, the countdown at F8162 alternates the request. With bit 01 or bit 80 set, the request bit is cleared. With none of these set, the request bit is set. The blink display uses the same request bit (8-3 Blink Code Display).

    The service manual documents the vehicle side. The PCM illuminates the MIL for codes that affect emissions; codes marked with one asterisk in the charts do not illuminate it, and codes marked with two asterisks illuminate it during engine operation (chart footnotes, page 25-7). The PCM turns off the MIL after three consecutive trips without the malfunction, except for the misfire and fuel system monitors, which use three successive tests without the malfunction near the operating condition at which it was first detected (Fig. 6).

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    READING STORED FAULTS

    Stored faults are read with the DRB scan tool on the Read Fault screen, or counted on the MIL after cycling the ignition On-Off-On-Off-On within five seconds (8-4 Entering Blink Code Mode). Both displays come from the stored-fault records described above. A fault in the record does not show that the condition is still present: use the monitor's own conditions and the DRB sensor and state displays to confirm the condition before repair (8-1 Diagnostic Overview).

    A monitor that is disabled in its table never produces a record. In the reference calibration this applies to twelve of the thirteen detailed monitors, fourteen of the twenty-four simple checks and nineteen of the thirty configured monitors. Check the enable tables before treating a missing code as proof that a system passed.

    BLINK CODE DISPLAY

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    BLINK CODE SERIALIZER

    The PCM displays stored trouble codes as two-digit flash codes on the malfunction indicator lamp (MIL). The blink code serializer (013EF4) produces the display. It owns the indicator request bit at F8107, bit 10, while blink mode is active, and it counts each code out as two groups of request changes.

    The serializer is called from the divided-rate service (01391E) when the low six bits of the runtime word equal 3E, and only while the engine running flag (F80D1, bit 40) is clear. Its pauses are deadlines on the restartable runtime word F8096, which the runtime counter service (029AD6) advances. Blink mode is armed by the arming count described in 8-4 Entering Blink Code Mode; the arming step sets the mode flag F8886, bit 04, and the first deadline.

    A display runs in a fixed order (Fig. 1). After an opening pause, the serializer selects an opening code, sends each stored code from the report list, and closes with code 55. When code 55 finishes, the serializer clears its stage flags in F810A and the mode flag, and the normal indicator policy takes the request bit back.

    OPENING CODE

    On the first pass after the arming deadline, the serializer sets the request bit, adds FF to the runtime word to form the opening pause, and clears the arming count F89A6. When that pause expires it marks the opening stage done (F810A, bit 02) and compares the low seven bits of retained byte F887C with the calibrated limit at ROM 120E, 40 (Fig. 2).

    Below the limit, the serializer loads code 12 and clears the request bit, which starts the first count. The service manual lists code 12 as the battery-disconnect indication (Fig. 5). At or above the limit, the serializer loads code 55 directly and sets the end flag (F810A, bit 01); the display then shows only the end marker.

    DIGIT COUNTING

    The working code is held at F8475 in packed decimal: code 31 is stored as 31. The serializer loads a progress byte at F8345 with the code plus 10, so the upper digit of the progress byte is one greater than the first digit of the code. Each serializer pass then acts on the progress byte as shown in the table and in Fig. 3.

    PROGRESS BYTEPASSACTION
    20 and aboveBit setClear request bit
    20 and aboveBit clearSet request bit; subtract 10 — one count, first digit
    10 to 1FOne passSubtract 10; request bit unchanged — separator
    01 to 0FBit setClear request bit
    01 to 0FBit clearSet request bit; subtract 1 — one count, second digit
    00—Pause to runtime + FF, then next code

    For code 31 the progress byte steps 41, 31, 21, 11 through three counts, takes 11 to 01 on the separator pass, and reaches 00 after one more count. Each count is one clear-and-set cycle of the request bit. The separator pass holds the request bit for one extra pass between the two digit groups, and the deadline at 00 holds it between codes.

    CODE CATALOG

    Stored faults are reported through an eight-entry list at F8868, kept in report order by the fault recorder (0150F8); refer to 8-2 Fault Reporting. When the progress byte reaches 00 and the code pause has expired, the serializer reads the list entry at index F8346. A zero entry, or an index of eight, selects code 55 and sets the end flag.

    A nonzero entry is a record number in the diagnostic code catalog at ROM 1222 (8-2, Fig. 4). Each record is three bytes: a two-byte generic scan tool code followed by the one-byte MIL code. The serializer reads the third byte, loads it as the working code, advances the list index and starts its first count on the same pass (Fig. 4).

    The record number is the HEX CODE column of the service manual chart, and the catalog bytes match its MIL CODE and GENERIC SCAN TOOL CODE columns. Records without a generic code carry 0000 in the first two bytes. Two records with the same MIL code display identically; the catalog maps battery temperature records P1492 and P1493 both to code 44.

    RECORDGENERIC CODEMIL CODEMANUAL DESCRIPTION
    01P034054No cam signal at PCM
    0A000042Auto shutdown relay control circuit
    12P044331EVAP purge solenoid circuit
    1EP011722ECT sensor voltage too low

    DISPLAY CANCEL AND INDICATOR HANDOFF

    The diagnostic indicator service (015054) leaves the request bit to the serializer while blink mode is active. If the first-engine-event flag (F80CE, bit 10), set by the engine event capture service (028F24), or the diagnostic flag F8109, bit 01, is set, the service cancels the display: it clears the mode flag, the arming count, the progress byte, the working code and the list index (8-2, Fig. 5). The first captured engine event therefore ends a display in progress. Outside blink mode the service applies the normal indicator policy from the fault flags in F8886 and the countdown at F8162.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    READING CODES WITH THE MIL

    Cycle the ignition key On-Off-On-Off-On within 5 seconds and count the MIL flashes (8-4, Fig. 1). The display starts with code 12 when the opening condition applies, shows each stored code once in report order, and ends with code 55. Keep the engine stopped: the serializer runs only while the engine running flag is clear, and the first engine event cancels the display.

    CODE CHART

    Codes 12 and 55 are produced by the serializer itself. Every other flash code comes from the third byte of a catalog record; refer to Fig. 5 for the opening rows of the manual chart.

    8 - 48 · ON-BOARD DIAGNOSTICSSR

    ENTERING BLINK CODE MODE

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    KEY-CYCLE PROCEDURE

    Diagnostic trouble codes can be read without a scan tool. The technician cycles the ignition key ON, OFF, ON, OFF, ON within five seconds, then counts the flashes of the malfunction indicator (check engine) lamp (Fig. 1). A short pause separates the two digits of a code; a longer pause separates codes. Code 12 reports that the direct battery input to the PCM was disconnected within the last 50 key-on cycles, and code 55 marks the end of the display (Fig. 7).

    In the PCM software, blink code mode starts from an arming count. Each accepted arming event adds one to a retained counter, and the third accepted event starts blink code mode. The count is kept in retained memory, so it carries across resets, while the startup-age word that limits when an event is accepted starts again from zero at every reset. This section describes how events reach the counter, the conditions that accept them, and the paths that clear the count. Code formatting and lamp timing are described in 8-3 Blink Code Display.

    ARMING EVENTS

    Arming events arrive as one-byte event codes. The companion-event router (018966) polls the companion link and, when a received byte is complete, files it in a working-memory mailbox chosen from a table of 27 offsets at ROM 07DC (Fig. 2). Event codes 27 and 28 share the arming mailbox F8331. A startup job (0194DE) qualifies the startup state and writes event 28 into the same mailbox directly, so the arming path serves both the link and the main processor.

    The shared diagnostic event service (018ECA) reads F8331 and marks the mailbox empty by writing FF. Event 27 clears the event latch F8492 bit 80 and sets F8106 bit 80. Event 28 queues coprocessor commands 84 and 86 when their request conditions are set (010028), then sets the latch F8492 bit 80, clears F8106 bit 80, and then tests the arming conditions (Fig. 3).

    ARMING CONDITIONS AND COUNT

    An event 28 advances the count only when four conditions hold. The high byte of the startup-age word F8098 must be zero, so the event must arrive before the word reaches 0100. Input port F0 bit 02 must be clear. The diagnostic flag F8109 bit 01 must be clear. Blink code mode, F8886 bit 04, must not already be active. An event that fails any condition leaves the count unchanged.

    An accepted event increments the retained byte F89A6 (Fig. 4). The byte wraps on overflow. When the new value is 3 or more, the service sets blink code mode, clears the digit progress byte F8345, clears the indicator request F8107 bit 10, and clears the working code F8475 and list index F8346. It also stores a start deadline in F8340: the restartable runtime word F8096 plus 01C6. The blink serializer (013EF4) holds the opening indication until the runtime word reaches this deadline.

    The runtime counter service (029AD6) advances both words. The startup-age word F8098 counts up and holds at FFFF. The runtime word F8096 counts up and, on overflow, rolls from FFFF to FF00.

    RETAINED COUNT AT RESET

    The reset routine (020000) sums the retained working memory (013D08) and compares the sum with the value stored at F8800. When the sum matches, the retained area F8800–F8A05 is kept, and the arming count in F89A6 keeps its value. When the sum does not match, the routine clears the retained area, which sets the count to zero, and then seeds its defaults. On both paths the routine then clears ordinary working memory F8000–F87FF, which returns the startup-age word and the runtime word to zero.

    The count therefore accumulates across consecutive resets, and each new startup opens a fresh acceptance window for the next event.

    CLEARING THE COUNT

    Outside reset, four software paths return the arming count to zero (Fig. 5):

    • Display start. When the serializer issues its opening indicator request, it clears the count.
    • Inactive threshold. When blink code mode is inactive and the startup-age word is at or above 005B, the serializer clears the count. The divided-rate service (01391E) calls the serializer only while the engine-running flag F80D1 bit 40 is clear.
    • Display cancellation. The diagnostic indicator service (015054) cancels an active display when the first-engine-event flag F80CE bit 10 is set by the capture routine (028F24), or when the diagnostic flag F8109 bit 01 is set. It clears blink code mode, the count, the progress byte, the working code and the list index (8-2, Fig. 5, 8-3 Blink Code Display).
    • Extended power-input hold. The power-input and retained-state shutdown service (013A66) clears the count on its extended hold path before it saves the retained-memory sum. Its shorter quiesce path saves the sum without clearing the count.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    OBTAINING CODES WITH THE MIL

    The service manual gives two ways to display trouble codes: the ignition key cycle and the DRB scan tool (Fig. 6). The DRB displays the codes through its Read Fault screen. Refer to 8-2 Fault Reporting for fault storage.

    FAULT SNAPSHOT AND HISTORY

    DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

    FAULT SNAPSHOT RECORD

    The PCM keeps one fault snapshot record, the freeze frame of the OBD request service. The record is fifteen bytes at F888A–F8898. It holds the internal id of the selected fault, the priority rank of the request that selected it and thirteen bytes of readings taken when the record was filled. The capture routine (014B52) fills the record. Six routines call it on a failure result: the failure handler (014A94), the history qualification (014E62), the observation dispatcher (018BB6), the simple-check qualification (018D28), the configured-monitor failure routine (01931A) and 0193C8 (8-2 Fault Reporting).

    The reading bytes F888B–F8896 are stored in the form the OBD request service (01E5E6) reports for the matching parameter. The snapshot record is separate from the stored-fault bitmap and the report-order list: it describes one fault, while the bitmap marks every stored fault and the list holds the order of up to eight.

    ADDRESSCONTENTSSOURCEPID
    F888AInternal fault idWorking fault id F847502
    F888BFuel system status 1Copy of F817503
    F888CFuel system status 2Copy of F817603
    F888DCalculated loadF8154 after the load calculation 014C9004
    F888ECoolant temperatureRaw coolant input F8034 through curve 0410, minus 24, limited at zero05
    F888FBank 1 short-term trimF828C, signed × 85 ÷ 256 + 12806
    F8890Bank 1 long-term trimF827E, same encoding07
    F8891Bank 2 short-term trimF828D, same encoding08
    F8892Bank 2 long-term trimF8280, same encoding09
    F8893PID 0A byteCopy of F829F0A

    F8898Priority rankRank passed by the caller—

    PID: OBD freeze-frame parameter that reads the byte. PID 0C sends the engine speed byte as its high byte with a zero low byte. PIDs 06 and 07 require ROM 270A bit 80, PIDs 08 and 09 require 270A bit 20, PID 0A requires ROM 2708 bit 80 and PID 0B requires 2708 bit 40 clear. The reference calibration stores A1 and 08, so the service does not answer PID 0A.

    REPLACEMENT RULE

    Each call to the capture routine carries a priority rank. The fault id comes from the working fault id F8475. The routine applies three tests in order (Fig. 1, Fig. 2):

    • A rank equal to or lower than the saved rank F8898 ends the call. The record is unchanged.
    • A higher rank is stored in F8898 at once. When the working fault id equals the saved id F888A, the call ends there: the rank rises and the readings stay as they were.
    • For a different fault id, the routine stores the id, copies the fuel system status bytes and builds the remaining readings.

    There is one record. A different fault at the same rank does not replace it, and a fault already in the record does not refresh its readings when its rank rises.

    The history qualification requests rank 1, or rank 2 when F8497 bit 20 is set. When the pending bit of the fault is already set, it sets the active bit, records the fault (0150F8) and adds 2, giving rank 3 or 4. The forced policy requests rank 3 in the failure handler, the observation dispatcher, the simple-check qualification and the configured-monitor failure routine. Routine 0193C8 requests rank 1, or rank 3 when F8889 bit 02 is set. Descriptor C020 requests rank 4 from the failure handler; that descriptor does not run in the reference calibration, whose detailed-monitor enable word is 0800 (8-1 Diagnostic Overview).

    SNAPSHOT READINGS

    After the gate, the capture routine runs the load calculation (014C90) and copies its result F8154. The coolant byte is converted from the raw coolant input F8034 through the thermistor curve at ROM 0410 (7-1, Fig. 4); the routine subtracts 24 and limits the result at zero (Fig. 4), the same conversion the live coolant parameter uses. It does not copy the working coolant temperature F80A6. When a coolant substitute is in use, the working temperature is the substitute while the snapshot holds the conversion of the sensor input (7-1 Substitute Values).

    The four fuel trim bytes are each multiplied as signed values by 85, and the high byte of the product is offset by 128. Vehicle speed F80A4 is multiplied by 206 and rounded to its high byte, the same conversion the live speed parameter uses. F829F and F812F are copied unchanged.

    The manifold pressure and engine speed bytes depend on the active monitor descriptor F8463. For descriptors C020 and C03C they come from the monitor cache at F8870; for C02E, the fuel correction monitor, from the cache at F8875. The cached pressure byte is scaled by 105 ÷ 256 or 34 ÷ 256. For other descriptors the routine converts the manifold pressure input F8044 and scales it by 34 ÷ 256, and takes the high byte of the engine speed word F805A. In each case the speed byte is shifted right once, so the snapshot holds engine speed in steps of 64 rpm: a reading of 800 rpm is stored as 768 rpm. The live engine speed parameter shifts the full speed word and keeps the finer value.

    SNAPSHOT REPORTING AND RELEASE

    The OBD request service reports the snapshot fault code under PID 02 only when the saved rank is 3 or higher (Fig. 5). Below rank 3 it reports a code word of zero. At rank 3 and above it reads the catalog record of the saved id, at ROM 1222 plus three times the id, and reports its code word (8-2 Fault Reporting). Saved id 76 (hex) reports P0172. The readings for PIDs 03 to 0D are reported from their bytes without a rank test.

    A clear result can release the record. While F887A holds a fault id, the clear handler (0149DE) clears the saved rank and the saved id when the rank is below 3 and the saved id equals the fault id that passed (Fig. 6). The readings stay in F888B–F8897 until the next capture or a full clear. A record at rank 3 or higher is not released by a clear result.

    WARM-UP COUNT

    The service manual states that the PCM erases a DTC after 40 warm-up cycles, and that a warm-up cycle is counted when coolant temperature has crossed 160 °F and has risen at least 40 °F since the engine started (Fig. 7). The software keeps a warm-up count in F887C.

    The descriptor monitor service (0147F0) calls the warm-up qualification (015220) after each detailed-monitor pass while F8802 bit 02 is clear (Fig. 8). The routine compares the working coolant temperature F80A6 with two limits and requires it to be above both:

    • The start reference F80A7 plus 22 °C, limited at FF.
    • 71 °C.

    With both met and bit 80 of F887C clear, the count in the low seven bits of F887C increases by one, up to 7F, and bit 80 latches the count. F8802 bit 02 is then set and the qualification is not called again. The startup routine (020000) clears F8802 bit 02 and both latch bits, so the count advances at most once per PCM startup. The start reference F80A7 is stored at initialization, by 026B84 and by the engine speed routine (026CFC). A coolant rise of exactly 22 °C, or a temperature of 71 °C, does not count.

    START COUNT AND RETEST SWEEP

    A second count, F887B, advances at most once per PCM startup after a delay with the engine running. The descriptor monitor service calls the start history routine (0152DC) at the end of each detailed-monitor pass while F887A holds a fault id. The routine reloads delay counter F833C with 42 while the running flag F80D1 bit 40 is clear. The countdown service (01F660) decrements the counter. With the engine running and the counter at zero, the routine increments the low seven bits of F887B, up to 7F, unless bit 80 has latched (Fig. 9).

    For start counts 1 to 3 the routine then runs a retest sweep. It places each nonzero fault id of the ROM table at 6FAF and each high and low fault id of the simple checks (ROM 70E2) in F8475 and advances its retest history (014F98), then latches bit 80. From count 4 the routine latches without a sweep. With the count at zero and the latch set, the sweep runs on each visit after the delay.

    A failure result resets both counts. The history qualification (014E62), the staged qualification (014DB8) and the fault record routine (0150F8) clear the low seven bits of F887C and F887B and set both latch bits. Neither count advances again until the next startup clears the latches.

    HISTORY AGING

    After each detailed-monitor pass the descriptor monitor service tests the two counts (Fig. 10, Fig. 11). Aging runs only when F887A holds a fault id and F8886 bit 80 is clear. The failure handler, the simple-check qualification and the configured-monitor failure routine store the failing fault id in F887A, and the full clear zeros it.

    • A warm-up count of 40 or more calls the full clear (00D00E).
    • Otherwise a start count of 80 or more calls the selected cleanup (015270).

    The aging test runs before the warm-up qualification and the start history routine in the same pass.

    FULL CLEAR

    The full clear routine erases the fault history and the snapshot. It is reached from three places: the aging test above, a clear request to the OBD request service (when F80CE bit 10 is clear) and the diagnostic command service (00C800). The service manual directs the technician to erase all DTCs with the DRB scan tool after a verified repair. The routine clears:

    WORKING MEMORYCLEARED
    F883F–F8846 *Four words loaded from ROM 7BA6, value 0000
    F89F0, F89F1, F8A02, F8A03 *Cleared
    F8902–F8981Packed retest history
    F888A–F8898Fault snapshot record
    F887AMost recent failing id
    F8868–F886FReport-order list
    F899A–F899CBytes shifted with each new report-order entry
    F8848–F8867Stored-fault bitmap
    F8870–F8879Monitor caches
    F887ECleared
    F8839 *Reloaded from ROM 6F29
    F887C *Warm-up count, low seven bits
    F8802 bit 80 *Cleared
    F8886 *Diagnostic flags
    F8808–F880E *Active fault flags

    The routine clears nothing when F80CE bit 10 is set together with F834E bit 80 or F8128 bit 01. Rows marked * run only when F834E bit 80 or F8128 bit 01 is set. The warm-up latch bit 80 and the start count F887B are not cleared.

    SELECTED CLEANUP

    The selected cleanup is lighter than the full clear. It zeros the ten monitor cache bytes F8870–F8879 and then reads two count-prefixed id lists, ROM 6DE3 and ROM 6DDE (Fig. 12, Fig. 13). For each id it clears only the pending bit in the packed history byte F8902 plus half the id: bit 10 for an even id, bit 01 for an odd id. The active bits 80 and 08 and the other history bits stay. The stored-fault bitmap, the report-order list and the snapshot are not changed.

    The first list holds 11 ids, the misfire codes P0300–P0310. The second holds 4 ids, the fuel correction codes (3-2 Fuel Feedback). The byte after the first list is outside its count and is not read.

    MONITOR-INCOMPLETE BYTE

    F8839 is the monitor-incomplete byte. The full clear reloads it from ROM 6F29, value 00. The incomplete-bit routine (014D0E) clears the bit that belongs to the active descriptor:

    DESCRIPTORBIT CLEARED
    C0BA01
    C0AC02
    C09E, C09004
    C06620
    C058, C07440
    C04A80

    Descriptor C090 clears bit 04 only when its state byte F850C bit 10 is set. Descriptors C058 and C074 share bit 40 and clear it only after a cross-check of the state bytes F8508 and F850A and F8886 bit 80. The OBD request service reports F8839 under PID 01; with F8883 bit 80 set it reports FF.

    DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

    READING THE SNAPSHOT

    • The snapshot holds the fault of the highest-ranked request since the last release or clear, not the most recent fault. A later request at the same rank does not replace it. Read all stored faults with the DRB (8-2 Fault Reporting).
    • A snapshot code of zero means the saved rank is below 3. The reading bytes still hold the last capture.
    • When a fault rises in rank, the readings remain those of its first capture.
    • Engine speed is stored in steps of 64 rpm.
    • The coolant reading is the conversion of the sensor input F8034. With a coolant fault flag set, the working temperature F80A6 holds the substitute value instead (7-1 Substitute Values).
    • A clear request to the OBD request service or the diagnostic command service runs the full clear: the snapshot, the stored-fault bitmap, the report-order list and the retest history are cleared. The warm-up count is cleared only when F834E bit 80 or F8128 bit 01 is set.
    • PID 0A is not answered in the reference calibration.
